title: Learning safely
subject: Digital safety
description: Learn how to study with a safe nickname and protect private information on shared devices.
content: A safe learning app should help children learn without asking for real names, document numbers, addresses, phone numbers, family details, or photos of private documents. Learners can use nicknames. If an app, website, or person asks for private information, stop and ask a trusted adult first.
goal: Use LearnBridge safely on a shared device without sharing private personal information.
steps: Look at the learner nickname box. Choose a short nickname, not a real full name.
Read these private examples together: phone number, exact location, ID document, family situation, and private photo.
Sort each example as safe for learning or private to protect.
Practice saying: I do not want to share that. I will ask my teacher.
Use the app without entering real names, documents, or location details.
practice: Make two columns on paper: OK for learning and Keep private. Put these words in the right column: nickname, favorite color, phone number, real full name, lesson progress, exact address, document photo.
checkQuestion: Which is safer to type in this app: a nickname or a real full name? Why?
teacherNote: Keep this lesson calm and practical. Do not ask children to reveal examples from their own family. UNICEF child online protection guidance emphasizes protecting children's identity and personal information online.

references.title: UNICEF: Online safety and data protection

title: Whole numbers and place value
subject: Math
description: Read, compare, and break apart whole numbers used in prices, distances, quantities, and records.
content: Place value tells us what each digit is worth. In 47,582, the digit 4 means forty thousand, while the digit 7 means seven thousand.
goal: Read and compare numbers up to 100,000 and identify the value of each digit.
realLifeUse: Use place value to understand prices, wages, population figures, distances, stock counts, and written records.

vocabulary.meaning: one symbol from 0 to 9 used to write numbers
the value a digit has because of its position

workedExamples.title: Compare 8,950 and 8,590
workedExamples.work: Both have 8 thousands. Compare hundreds: 9 hundreds is greater than 5 hundreds, so 8,950 > 8,590.

steps: Read 26,407 aloud: twenty-six thousand, four hundred and seven.
Identify each place from right to left: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands.
Compare two numbers from the largest place first.
Order 3,450, 3,405, and 3,540 from smallest to largest.
practice: Find three large numbers on a receipt, package, sign, or newspaper. Read each number, break it into place values, and arrange the three numbers from smallest to largest.

exercises.question: What is the value of 7 in 47,582?
exercises.explanation: The 7 is in the thousands place, so its value is 7,000.

exercises.question: Which number is greatest?
exercises.explanation: All have 9 thousands. Comparing hundreds and then tens shows 9,450 is greatest.

exercises.question: Which expanded form equals 30,608?
exercises.explanation: 30,608 contains 30,000, 600, no tens, and 8 ones.

finalTask: Imagine you manage supplies for a learning centre. The stock records show 12,450 notebooks, 12,405 pencils, and 10,980 sheets of paper. Read each number aloud, write its expanded form, and arrange the quantities from greatest to smallest.
takeaway: A digit's position determines its value.
Compare numbers from the largest place first.
Expanded form makes each place value visible.
checkQuestion: Can you explain why 12,450 is greater than 12,405?
teacherNote: Use locally familiar prices and quantities. Ask learners to explain their comparison rather than only naming the answer.

title: Money, totals, and change
subject: Math
description: Add prices, check a total, and calculate the correct change during everyday purchases.
content: A purchase has three important numbers: the price, the amount paid, and the change. Change = amount paid - total price.
goal: Calculate a shopping total and verify change using addition and subtraction.
realLifeUse: Use this skill at markets, shops, transport counters, and anywhere you pay with cash.

vocabulary.meaning: the amount after adding all prices
money returned when you pay more than the total

workedExamples.title: Find a total
workedExamples.work: Rice: 35 baht + eggs: 28 baht = 63 baht total.

workedExamples.title: Find the change
workedExamples.work: 100 baht paid - 63 baht total = 37 baht change.

workedExamples.title: Check the answer
workedExamples.work: 63 total + 37 change = 100 paid.

steps: Write each price in a vertical list with place values aligned.
Add the prices to find the total.
Subtract the total from the amount paid.
Check by adding the total and change; they should equal the amount paid.
Estimate first so you can notice an unreasonable answer.
practice: Make a small shop using three objects and paper price labels. One person buys two items and pays with a chosen amount. The other calculates and checks the change. Switch roles.

exercises.question: A meal costs 45 baht and water costs 12 baht. What is the total?
You pay 100 baht for a 57-baht purchase. What change should you receive?
Which calculation checks 25 baht change from a 75-baht purchase paid with 100 baht?
exercises.explanation: The purchase total plus the change must equal the amount paid.

finalTask: Plan a purchase of three useful items with prices of your choice. Find the total, choose an amount to pay, calculate the change, and prove your answer by adding the total and change.
takeaway: Add every price to find the total.
Subtract the total from the amount paid to find change.
Check that total + change = amount paid.
Estimate before calculating.
checkQuestion: Can you calculate and verify the change from a two-item purchase?
teacherNote: Use a familiar local currency and realistic prices. Emphasize checking change rather than mental speed.

title: Measure everyday objects
subject: Math
description: Choose suitable units and measure length, mass, and liquid volume.
content: Measurements need both a number and a unit. A table might be 120 centimetres long, a rice bag 5 kilograms, and a water bottle 1 litre.
goal: Choose suitable metric units and make reasonable everyday measurements.
realLifeUse: Use measurement for cooking, building, sewing, transport, health, buying goods, and organising a room.

vocabulary.meaning: how long or tall something is
how much liquid a container holds
a sensible answer made before exact measuring

workedExamples.title: Length
workedExamples.work: A pencil is about 15 centimetres. A road distance is measured in kilometres.

workedExamples.title: Mass
workedExamples.work: A small food packet may be 500 grams. A rice bag may be 5 kilograms.

workedExamples.title: Volume
workedExamples.work: A small drink may be 250 millilitres. A large bottle may hold 2 litres.

steps: Decide what is being measured: length, mass, or liquid volume.
Choose a suitable unit: mm, cm, m, km, g, kg, mL, or L.
Estimate the measurement before using a tool.
Start the ruler or measuring tool at zero.
Record the number and unit, then compare it with your estimate.
practice: Estimate and then measure three available objects. Record the object, your estimate, the measured result, and the difference. If no tools are available, compare objects using hand spans or equal containers and label the result as informal measurement.

exercises.question: Which unit is best for the length of a classroom?
exercises.explanation: Metres measure the length of a room-sized space.

exercises.question: Which unit is suitable for a bag of rice?
exercises.explanation: Kilograms are used for the mass of heavier everyday items.

exercises.question: A bottle holds 1,000 millilitres. How many litres is that?
exercises.explanation: 1,000 millilitres equals 1 litre.

finalTask: Choose one task: plan the length of a shelf, divide 2 litres of water into equal containers, or compare the mass of three food packages. State the correct units, estimate first, then calculate or measure the result.
takeaway: Always write a unit with a measurement.
Choose a unit that fits the object and purpose.
Estimate first, then measure and compare.
checkQuestion: Can you choose suitable units for length, mass, and volume?
teacherNote: Use available measuring tools, packages, and containers. Clearly distinguish informal estimates from standard metric measurements.

title: Fractions, percentages, and discounts
subject: Math
description: Understand common fractions and calculate simple percentages and sale prices.
content: Fractions and percentages describe parts of a whole. One half equals 50%, one quarter equals 25%, and one tenth equals 10%.
goal: Connect common fractions to percentages and calculate 10%, 25%, and 50% of an amount.
realLifeUse: Use percentages for discounts, savings, phone data, test scores, recipes, and sharing quantities fairly.

vocabulary.meaning: a number that represents part of a whole
an amount removed from the original price

workedExamples.title: Find a discounted price
workedExamples.work: 500 original price - 50 discount = 450 final price.

workedExamples.title: Use a common fraction
workedExamples.work: 50% is one half, so 50% of 80 = 80 ÷ 2 = 40.

steps: Identify the whole amount or original price.
Translate common percentages: 50% = one half, 25% = one quarter, 10% = one tenth.
Divide the whole to find the percentage amount.
For a discount, subtract the discount amount from the original price.
Check that the discounted price is smaller than the original price.
practice: Create price labels for 200, 400, and 800. Calculate a 10% discount for each. Then choose one price and calculate a 25% and 50% discount.

exercises.question: What is 10% of 600?
An item costs 500 with a 10% discount. What is the final price?
exercises.explanation: 10% of 500 is 50. Subtract 50 from 500 to get 450.

exercises.question: Which percentage is equal to one quarter?
exercises.explanation: One whole has four quarters, so one quarter is 25 out of 100, or 25%.

finalTask: A shop lists a bag at 800 with a 25% discount. Calculate the discount and final price. Then compare it with a different offer of 100 off. Explain which offer saves more.
takeaway: Percent means out of 100.
10% is one tenth, 25% is one quarter, and 50% is one half.
Discounted price = original price - discount.
Compare actual money saved, not only the advertised words.
checkQuestion: Can you calculate a simple discount and explain the result?
teacherNote: Use simple whole-number prices first. Allow calculators after learners can explain which operation they need and why.

title: Everyday mathematics checkpoint
subject: Math
description: Use whole numbers, money, measurement, and percentages to plan a realistic weekly budget.
content: This checkpoint combines the four mathematics lessons. Read the scenario carefully, choose the needed operations, and check whether each answer is reasonable.
goal: Plan purchases within a fixed budget and explain each calculation.
realLifeUse: Use this process to plan food, transport, phone credit, supplies, or another short-term budget.

workedExamples.title: Example weekly plan
workedExamples.work: Budget 600. Rice 180 + vegetables 90 + transport 60 + phone 120 = 450 spent. 600 - 450 = 150 remaining.

workedExamples.title: Check
workedExamples.work: 450 spent + 150 remaining = 600 total budget.

steps: Write the total budget.
List every planned cost using the same currency unit.
Add the costs to find total spending.
Subtract spending from the budget to find the remaining amount.
Check the result and decide whether the plan needs adjustment.

exercises.question: Using the example plan, what is the total spending?
How much remains from the 600 budget?
exercises.explanation: 600 - 450 = 150 remaining.

exercises.question: Phone credit has a 10% discount from 120. What is the discount?
A 2-litre bottle contains how many millilitres?
exercises.explanation: Each litre has 1,000 millilitres, so 2 litres = 2,000 millilitres.

finalTask: Create your own budget using at least four costs. Include one discounted item and one measured quantity. Calculate spending, savings, and the remaining balance. Check that spending plus the remaining balance equals the original budget, then explain one choice you would change if costs increased.
takeaway: Write the problem clearly before calculating.
Use the correct operation and units.
Estimate so unreasonable answers are easier to notice.
Check calculations using a second operation whenever possible.
checkQuestion: Can you create and verify a budget that does not exceed the available amount?
teacherNote: Invite learners to choose realistic but fictional amounts. The goal is mathematical planning, not collecting private financial information.

title: Meet the Thai writing system
subject: Thai language
description: See how consonants, vowels, tone information, and syllables work together.
content: Thai is written from left to right, but vowel symbols may appear before, after, above, or below a consonant. Learn the system in small sound groups instead of memorizing every symbol at once.
goal: Identify the main parts of written Thai and explain why spelling carries pronunciation information.
realLifeUse: Use this map when reading signs, names, lesson books, transport information, and dictionary entries.

workedExamples.title: One written syllable
workedExamples.work: กา combines consonant ก with long vowel า. The parts are read together as one syllable.

workedExamples.title: A vowel can be written first
workedExamples.work: In เก, vowel symbol เ- is written before consonant ก even though the consonant sound begins the syllable.

steps: Find the consonant in กา.
Find the vowel in กา.
Compare กา with เก and notice the vowel position.
Copy both while naming the consonant and vowel parts.
practice: Use two colours to mark consonants and vowels in a few teacher-checked syllables.

exercises.question: Where can a Thai vowel symbol appear?
options: Before, after, above, or below a consonant
exercises.explanation: Thai vowel symbols can be written in several positions around a consonant.

finalTask: Label the consonant and vowel parts in three teacher-checked Thai syllables.
takeaway: Thai is written left to right.
Written vowel position is not always sound order.
Learn symbols together with their sounds.
checkQuestion: Can you point out a consonant and vowel in a simple syllable?
teacherNote: This is an orientation, not a complete alphabet chart. Verify every example with a fluent Thai reader.

title: Consonant sounds and classes
subject: Thai language
description: Learn why Thai consonants belong to mid, high, and low tone classes.
content: Thai traditionally lists 44 consonant symbols; two are obsolete in modern use. They represent 21 initial consonant sounds and belong to three classes that help determine tone.
goal: Recognize a starter set of consonants and understand the purpose of consonant classes.
realLifeUse: Consonant class is needed later when working out the tone of a written syllable.

vocabulary.term: ก จ ด ต บ ป อ
vocabulary.meaning: A starter selection of mid-class consonants

workedExamples.title: Same initial sound, different class
workedExamples.work: ข and ค both begin with an aspirated kh sound, but ข is high class and ค is low class.

workedExamples.title: Initial and final sounds
workedExamples.work: Some letters have a different final sound, so learn them in real syllables as well as in the alphabet.

steps: Listen to five selected consonants.
Trace each while saying its sound.
Sort them into mid, high, or low class using a chart.
Find them in short printed words.
practice: Make cards with the symbol on one side and its class and sound on the other. Study five at a time.

exercises.question: Why do consonant classes matter?
exercises.explanation: Consonant class is one factor used to determine a written syllable's tone.

finalTask: Identify the sound and class of five consonants from your current study set.
takeaway: There are more symbols than initial consonant sounds.
The three classes are mid, high, and low.
Study a small cumulative set.
checkQuestion: Can you explain the difference between consonant sound and class?
teacherNote: Do not require all 44 symbols at once. Build a cumulative chart and teach initial and final sounds in context.

title: Vowels and vowel length
subject: Thai language
description: Recognize common vowel shapes, positions, and short-long contrasts.
content: Thai vowel forms are written around a consonant placeholder. Vowel length can distinguish words and can matter when applying tone rules.
goal: Read and contrast a starter set of short and long vowel patterns.
realLifeUse: Accurate vowel length makes spoken words easier to understand and supports reading.

vocabulary.meaning: A vowel written before its consonant

workedExamples.title: Short and long
workedExamples.work: Listen carefully: a short vowel and its long partner can distinguish words.

workedExamples.title: The dash is a placeholder
workedExamples.work: In a chart, the dash in เ- shows where the consonant belongs.

steps: Listen to one short-long pair.
Repeat without changing the consonant.
Identify the vowel position.
Copy the pair and underline the changing vowel.
practice: Hear a teacher-checked syllable and point to the short or long vowel card you hear.

exercises.question: Why should learners notice vowel length?
options: It can affect meaning and tone rules
exercises.explanation: Vowel length can distinguish words and is relevant in some tone rules.

finalTask: Identify short or long vowels in four teacher-checked syllables and copy each pattern.
takeaway: Vowels can surround a consonant.
Short and long vowels contrast.
Connect every written vowel with trusted audio.
checkQuestion: Can you identify one short-long pair in writing and by listening?
teacherNote: Use recordings or a fluent model. Keep one romanization system within a lesson.

title: Five tones and four tone marks
subject: Thai language
description: Hear the five spoken tones and learn why a tone mark alone does not give the answer.
content: Standard Thai distinguishes five spoken tones: mid, low, falling, high, and rising. Thai uses four written tone marks, but spoken tone also depends on consonant class, syllable type, and sometimes vowel length.
goal: Name the five tones, recognize the four marks, and use a tone chart instead of guessing.
realLifeUse: Tone can distinguish meaning, so listening practice improves understanding and speech.

vocabulary.term: เสียงสามัญ
เสียงจัตวา

workedExamples.title: Five sounds, four marks
workedExamples.work: A syllable can have no tone mark and still carry one of the five spoken tones.

workedExamples.title: The mark is not the whole rule
workedExamples.work: The same mark can produce different spoken tones with different consonant classes.

workedExamples.title: Live and dead syllables
workedExamples.work: Classify the syllable before applying a tone rule.

steps: Listen to five tones on a controlled syllable set.
Trace pitch movement with your hand.
Match the four mark shapes to their names.
Use a chart on one syllable: class, live or dead, mark, then spoken tone.
Check against trusted audio.
practice: Listen to two versions of a syllable and decide whether the pitch movement is the same or different before reading labels.

exercises.question: How many spoken tones are commonly described in Standard Thai?
exercises.explanation: Standard Thai is commonly described with five spoken tones.

exercises.question: Is a tone mark enough by itself?
options: No; consonant class and syllable type also matter
exercises.explanation: Use consonant class, syllable type, the mark, and relevant vowel length.

finalTask: Use a chart to analyse three teacher-checked syllables and verify each spoken tone against audio.
takeaway: The five tones are mid, low, falling, high, and rising.
There are four written tone marks.
Apply the complete rule and confirm by listening.
checkQuestion: Why do five spoken tones not require five written marks?

resourceGuide.title: Use an interactive tone chart while online
resourceGuide.description: SEAsite provides charts and playable examples. Use notes or legally downloaded course files offline.
steps: Listen before looking at the label.
Compare one pattern across tones.
Record class and syllable type.
Ask a fluent speaker to check production.

teacherNote: Do not reduce tones to arrows alone. Learners need repeated listening discrimination and fluent feedback.

title: Greet people politely
subject: Thai language
description: Use a greeting, polite particle, thanks, and a simple clarification phrase.
content: Thai is tonal, so written approximations cannot show pronunciation completely. Listen to a trusted speaker or recording, copy the sound, and use the writing as a reminder.
goal: Greet someone, thank them, and say that you do not understand.
realLifeUse: Use these phrases when meeting a teacher, neighbour, coworker, shop worker, or community helper.

vocabulary.meaning: Polite sentence-ending particles; usage commonly depends on the speaker

vocabulary.term: ไม่เข้าใจ (mai khao jai)

patterns: สวัสดีครับ / สวัสดีค่ะ
ขอบคุณครับ / ขอบคุณค่ะ
ขอโทษครับ / ขอโทษค่ะ
ไม่เข้าใจครับ / ไม่เข้าใจค่ะ

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: สวัสดีครับ / สวัสดีค่ะ (Hello.)

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: สวัสดีครับ / สวัสดีค่ะ

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: [A short instruction in Thai]

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: ขอโทษครับ / ค่ะ ไม่เข้าใจครับ / ค่ะ (Sorry, I do not understand.)

steps: Listen to a trusted Thai speaker or recording before reading the romanization.
Repeat the greeting and thanks three times at a comfortable speed.
Practise adding the polite particle used by the speaker.
Role-play hearing an instruction and saying that you do not understand.
practice: Take turns greeting someone, receiving a short instruction, saying you do not understand, and thanking the speaker after they repeat it.

exercises.question: Which phrase means 'I do not understand'?
exercises.explanation: ไม่เข้าใจ means 'I do not understand.'

finalTask: Complete a four-line exchange: greet, listen, say you do not understand, and thank the other person.
takeaway: Thai tones affect meaning, so listen as well as read.
Polite particles make short phrases more courteous.
It is better to ask than to pretend you understood.
checkQuestion: Can you greet someone and say that you do not understand?
teacherNote: Ask a fluent Thai speaker to review pronunciation and local usage. Explain polite particles carefully and respectfully; do not force learners into a gender label.

references.title: SEAsite Spoken Thai: greetings and general phrases

title: Ask for basic needs and help
subject: Thai language
description: Ask for water, food, a toilet, or help using short phrases and visual support.
content: A few well-practised requests are more useful than a long word list. Combine speech with pointing, a picture card, or a written place name.
goal: Make a simple request for an immediate everyday need.
realLifeUse: Use these phrases at home, class, work, a clinic, a food stall, or while travelling.

vocabulary.term: ช่วยด้วย (chuai duai)
อยู่ที่ไหน (yu thi nai)

patterns: ขอน้ำหน่อยครับ / ค่ะ — Water, please.
ห้องน้ำอยู่ที่ไหนครับ / คะ — Where is the toilet?
ช่วยด้วยครับ / ค่ะ — Please help.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.text: ขอโทษครับ / ค่ะ ห้องน้ำอยู่ที่ไหนครับ / คะ (Excuse me, where is the toilet?)

dialogue.speaker: Helper
dialogue.text: อยู่ทางซ้าย (It is on the left.)

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.text: ขอบคุณครับ / ค่ะ (Thank you.)

steps: Match each Thai word to a picture.
Listen and repeat one complete request.
Practise pointing to a picture while making the request.
Finish the exchange with thanks.
practice: Use four picture cards: water, food, toilet, and help. Draw a card and make the matching request without showing private information.

exercises.question: Which phrase asks where the toilet is?
options: ห้องน้ำอยู่ที่ไหน
exercises.explanation: ห้องน้ำ means toilet and อยู่ที่ไหน asks where it is.

finalTask: Choose one need, get a person's attention politely, make the request, use a picture if needed, and thank the person.
takeaway: Pointing or a picture can support speech.
Use ช่วยด้วย for an urgent request for help.
Repeat the location back or check a sign when possible.
checkQuestion: Can you ask for one basic need using words and a visual clue?
teacherNote: A fluent Thai speaker must check pronunciation and whether phrases fit the local context. Do not treat this lesson as emergency-response training.

references.title: SEAsite Spoken Thai: directions and useful phrases

title: Shop and check a price
subject: Thai language
description: Ask how much something costs, understand the purpose of a price response, and choose an item.
content: Shopping practice combines language with everyday mathematics. Always check written prices and calculate totals rather than relying on speech alone.
goal: Ask a price and complete a simple practice purchase.
realLifeUse: Use this at a market, food stall, pharmacy, stationery shop, or ticket counter.

vocabulary.term: เท่าไหร่ (thao rai)
เอาอันนี้ (ao an ni)

patterns: อันนี้เท่าไหร่ครับ / คะ — How much is this?
เอาอันนี้ครับ / ค่ะ — I will take this one.
ไม่เอาครับ / ค่ะ — I will not take it.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: ขอโทษครับ / ค่ะ อันนี้เท่าไหร่ครับ / คะ (Excuse me, how much is this?)

dialogue.speaker: Seller
dialogue.text: ห้าสิบบาท (50 baht.)

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: เอาอันนี้ครับ / ค่ะ (I will take this one.)

steps: Place written prices on three practice items.
Ask the price of one item.
Compare the spoken answer with the written price.
Choose the item or politely decline.
Calculate the expected change before paying.
practice: Run a small pretend market using fictional money. Swap customer and seller roles after each purchase.

exercises.question: Which phrase asks 'How much is this?'
options: อันนี้เท่าไหร่
ห้องน้ำอยู่ที่ไหน
exercises.explanation: อันนี้ means 'this one' and เท่าไหร่ asks how much.

finalTask: Ask the price, verify it against a label, decide whether to buy, and check the change for one practice item.
takeaway: Check written prices.
Use the maths course to practise totals and change.
You can politely decide not to buy.
checkQuestion: Can you ask a price and verify a simple purchase total?
teacherNote: Use familiar low-risk items and fictional prices. A fluent speaker should review pronunciation, particles, and natural wording.

references.title: SEAsite Quick Thai: shopping and numbers

title: Ask for a place or transport
subject: Thai language
description: Ask where a place is and confirm a simple left, right, or straight-ahead direction.
content: Directions work best when speech is supported by a map, destination card, transport number, or landmark.
goal: Ask where a place is and identify three basic direction words.
realLifeUse: Use this for a school, clinic, station, bus stop, workplace, toilet, or another public place.

vocabulary.term: อยู่ที่ไหน (yu thi nai)

patterns: [place] อยู่ที่ไหนครับ / คะ — Where is [place]?
ไป [place] ไหมครับ / คะ — Does it go to [place]?
ซ้าย / ขวา / ตรงไป — left / right / straight

dialogue.speaker: Traveller
dialogue.text: ขอโทษครับ / ค่ะ สถานีรถไฟอยู่ที่ไหนครับ / คะ (Where is the railway station?)

dialogue.speaker: Helper
dialogue.text: ตรงไป แล้วเลี้ยวซ้าย (Go straight, then turn left.)

dialogue.speaker: Traveller
dialogue.text: ขอบคุณครับ / ค่ะ

steps: Write or show the destination.
Ask where it is.
Listen for left, right, or straight.
Point on a simple map and repeat the direction.
Confirm against signs or a route number.
practice: Place three destinations on a small map. One person asks; the other gives a one- or two-step direction.

exercises.question: Which word means right?
exercises.explanation: ขวา means right; ซ้าย means left.

finalTask: Use a map to ask for one destination, follow a two-step direction, and point to the correct place.
takeaway: Show the destination as well as saying it.
Repeat the direction and point on a map.
Verify real transport routes separately.
checkQuestion: Can you ask where a place is and recognize left, right, and straight?
teacherNote: This teaches language, not verified travel information. Replace destinations with useful local examples and confirm real routes independently.

title: Practical Thai checkpoint
subject: Thai language
description: Combine greetings, basic needs, shopping, and directions in short real-life role-plays.
content: The checkpoint measures whether a learner can complete a useful task. Perfect spelling, tone, or speed is not required, but pronunciation should keep improving with trusted audio and feedback.
goal: Complete four short practical exchanges with speech and visual support.
realLifeUse: Use this review to decide which phrases are ready and which need another round of listening practice.
steps: Greet someone and say you do not understand.
Ask for water, a toilet, or help.
Ask an item's price and verify it.
Ask where a place is and follow a direction.
Review and retry any unclear task.
practice: Create four stations using picture cards, labelled objects, fictional money, and a simple map. Swap roles at every station.

exercises.question: You need the toilet. Which question is useful?
options: อันนี้เท่าไหร่
ห้องน้ำอยู่ที่ไหน
exercises.explanation: ห้องน้ำอยู่ที่ไหน asks where the toilet is.

exercises.question: You did not understand the answer. What should you do?
options: Ask again and show a picture or map
exercises.explanation: Ask again and use visual support to reduce misunderstanding.

finalTask: Complete two role-plays without reading every line: one basic-needs or directions task and one shopping task. Use a polite greeting and thanks.
takeaway: Listening practice is essential for a tonal language.
Pictures, maps, numbers, and signs support communication.
A fluent speaker should correct pronunciation before real use.
checkQuestion: Which real-life task can you now complete, and which needs more listening practice?

resourceGuide.title: Prepare trusted Thai materials for offline study
resourceGuide.description: LearnBridge provides a practical sequence. Use the original providers for fuller lessons, Thai script, and pronunciation practice.
steps: While online, open the Royal Thai Consulate textbook library and choose an appropriate beginner book or workbook.
Download the PDF to the device and test that it opens before going offline.
Use SEAsite while connected for spoken examples and repeat them with a fluent speaker when possible.
Keep the original provider name and link with every downloaded resource.

teacherNote: Complete a fluent-speaker review before field use. The linked textbook library and SEAsite materials remain with their original providers; verify their current terms before redistributing files.

references.title: Royal Thai Consulate-General Los Angeles: Thai textbook library
Northern Illinois University SEAsite Thai materials

title: Reading practice
subject: Literacy
description: Practice reading short sentences, pointing to words, and changing one word to make meaning.
content: Reading grows through small repeated practice. In this lesson, learners read a short sentence, point to each word, copy it if paper is available, and change one word to make a new sentence.
goal: Read a short sentence with support, identify words, and change one word to create a new sentence.
steps: Teacher reads first: I can learn today.
Learners read together slowly three times.
Point to each word while reading: I / can / learn / today.
Ask: Which word tells what we do? Which word tells when?
Change one word to make a new sentence, such as: I can count today, I can read today, or We can learn today.
practice: Learners work with a partner. One reads the sentence. One points to the words. Then they choose one word to change and read the new sentence together.
checkQuestion: Read your new sentence. Which word did you change?
teacherNote: Use shared reading before individual reading. Global Digital Library focuses on accessible early grade reading resources in languages children use and understand.

references.title: Global Digital Library: early reading resources
UNESCO: Global Digital Library and early reading

title: English greetings
subject: English
description: Practice simple English greetings for meeting teachers, helpers, and classmates.
content: Practice these greetings: Hello. My name is ___. Thank you. Please help me. Say each phrase slowly. Then practice with a partner using a safe nickname instead of a real full name.
goal: Practice simple English phrases for greetings and asking for help.
realLifeUse: Use these phrases when arriving at a class, meeting a new person, thanking someone, or asking a teacher or worker for help.

vocabulary.meaning: a greeting used when you meet someone
a polite word used when asking

patterns: Hello. My name is ___.
Nice to meet you.
Please help me.
Thank you for your help.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Hello. My name is Lin. What is your name?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: My name is May. Nice to meet you.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Nice to meet you too.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Please help me find the classroom.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Yes. It is this way.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Thank you for your help.

steps: Say together: Hello.
Say together: My name is ___. Use a safe nickname.
Say together: Thank you.
Say together: Please help me.
Practice a short greeting with a partner.
practice: Learners practice a two-line conversation: Hello. My name is ___. Hello. Please help me. They can use safe nicknames only.

exercises.question: What is the best phrase when meeting someone for the first time?
exercises.explanation: 'Nice to meet you' is a polite response during a first introduction.

exercises.question: Choose the polite request.
exercises.explanation: Adding 'please' makes the request polite and natural.

exercises.question: What can you say after someone helps you?
exercises.explanation: Use 'Thank you for your help' to show appreciation.

finalTask: Imagine it is your first day in a new class. Greet one person, introduce yourself with a nickname, ask for help finding the classroom, and thank them. Practice until you can say all four parts without reading.
takeaway: Begin with 'Hello.'
Use 'Nice to meet you' during a first introduction.
Use 'Please help me' for a polite request.
Thank the person after receiving help.
checkQuestion: What English phrase can you use when you need help?
teacherNote: Let learners practice in pairs after group repetition. Remind them that nicknames are enough for learning activities.

title: Introduce yourself
subject: English
description: Build a short introduction using a name, where you are from, and one interest.
content: A simple introduction helps people begin a conversation at school, work, or in a new community. Use a nickname when you do not need to share your legal name.
goal: Say and understand a simple three-sentence personal introduction.
realLifeUse: Use this skill when meeting a classmate, joining a course, speaking to a volunteer, or beginning a job interview.

vocabulary.meaning: the place where you began or grew up
to have your home in a place
to use a language when talking
wanting to learn or know more about something

patterns: My name is ___.
I am from ___.
I live in ___.
I speak ___ and ___.
I am interested in ___.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Hello. My name is Maya. What is your name?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Hi, Maya. I am Ko. Nice to meet you.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Nice to meet you too. Where are you from?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: I am from Myanmar, and I live in Thailand now.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: What are you interested in?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: I am interested in computers and English.

steps: Read aloud: Hello. My name is Maya.
Add a place: I am from Myanmar.
Add one interest: I like music.
Join the sentences: Hello. My name is Maya. I am from Myanmar. I like music.
Ask a partner: What is your name? What do you like?
practice: Choose a nickname, a country or town, and one interest. Say your introduction twice. On the second try, look up from the screen and speak from memory.

exercises.question: Which sentence tells someone your current home?
exercises.explanation: Use 'I live in ...' for the place where your home is now.

exercises.question: Choose the best reply to: What are you interested in?
exercises.explanation: 'I am interested in ...' introduces a subject or activity you want to learn more about.

exercises.question: Complete the sentence: I ___ Burmese and English.
exercises.explanation: We use 'speak' before the name of a language.

finalTask: Imagine you are joining a new class. Prepare a five-sentence introduction using your name or nickname, where you are from, where you live now, the languages you speak, and one interest. Say it aloud without reading every word. Then ask another person two questions: What is your name? What are you interested in?
takeaway: Use 'I am from ...' for your place of origin.
Use 'I live in ...' for your current home.
Use 'I speak ...' for languages.
Use 'I am interested in ...' for interests or learning goals.
checkQuestion: Can you introduce yourself using three short sentences?
teacherNote: Model the introduction first. Learners may replace the place sentence with 'I live in ___' or skip it if they prefer not to share that information.

title: Ask when you do not understand
subject: English
description: Practice useful questions for lessons, instructions, and everyday conversations.
content: Asking a clear question is a learning skill. These short phrases help when someone speaks too quickly or an instruction is unclear.
goal: Use four polite phrases to ask for repetition, meaning, or help.
realLifeUse: Use these questions in a classroom, workplace, clinic, shop, or public office when instructions are unclear.

vocabulary.meaning: to know the meaning of something
to say or do something again
at a speed that is easier to follow
to have a particular definition or message

patterns: I do not understand.
Could you say that again, please?
Could you speak more slowly, please?
What does ___ mean?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: Please submit the form before noon.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.text: I do not understand. What does submit mean?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: It means give the completed form to me.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.text: Could you say the time again, please?

dialogue.speaker: Teacher
dialogue.text: Before twelve o'clock.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.text: Thank you. I understand now.

steps: Say: I do not understand.
Say: Please say that again.
Say: Please speak slowly.
Ask: What does this mean?
Practice choosing the best phrase for a fast speaker, a new word, and a difficult instruction.
practice: Partner A reads a short instruction quickly. Partner B asks them to repeat or speak slowly. Switch roles, then use 'What does this mean?' for one unfamiliar word.

exercises.question: Someone speaks too fast. What should you ask?
options: Could you speak more slowly, please?
exercises.explanation: Ask the speaker to slow down when speed is the problem.

exercises.question: You hear an unfamiliar word. Which question is most useful?
exercises.explanation: Ask what a word means when you need its definition.

exercises.question: Which request is the most polite?
options: Could you say that again, please?
exercises.explanation: 'Could you ... please?' is a polite request pattern.

finalTask: Ask another person to give you a two-step instruction. Use at least two clarification phrases before repeating the instruction back in your own words. Finish with: I understand now. Thank you.
takeaway: Say clearly when you do not understand.
Ask for repetition when you missed the message.
Ask for slower speech when speed is the problem.
Ask what a word means when vocabulary is the problem.
checkQuestion: What can you say when someone is speaking too quickly?
teacherNote: Treat asking questions as a positive skill. Allow learners to read the phrases from the screen until they become comfortable.

title: Signs and simple directions
subject: English
description: Recognize common signs and follow short directions in schools, stations, clinics, and public places.
content: A few common words can make public places easier to understand. Focus on meaning first, then practice giving and following one-step directions.
goal: Recognize six common signs and follow four basic direction words.
realLifeUse: Use this skill to find entrances, exits, toilets, information desks, clinics, and transport stops.

vocabulary.meaning: the place where you go into a building
the place where you leave a building
a place where you can ask questions
the two directions on either side of you

patterns: Where is the ___?
Go straight.
Turn left / Turn right.
It is next to the ___.
It is across from the ___.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Excuse me. Where is the information desk?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Go straight and turn right.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Is it next to the entrance?

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: Yes. It is across from the ticket office.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: You're welcome.

steps: Read the signs: Entrance, Exit, Toilet, Information, Hospital, and Bus stop.
Practice the directions: left, right, straight, and stop.
Say: Go straight. Turn left. Turn right. Stop here.
Draw a simple map with a start point and one destination.
Guide a partner across the map using two or three short directions.
practice: Place three paper labels around the room, such as Exit, Information, and Bus stop. One learner asks, 'Where is the bus stop?' Another gives a simple direction using left, right, or straight.

exercises.question: Which sign shows the way out of a building?
exercises.explanation: An exit is the place where you leave a building.

exercises.question: Which question asks for a location?
exercises.explanation: Use 'Where is ...?' to ask for the location of a place.

exercises.question: What does 'go straight' mean?
exercises.explanation: 'Go straight' means continue forward without turning left or right.

finalTask: Draw a small map containing an entrance, information desk, toilet, and bus stop. Ask a partner for one location, then guide them with at least three direction phrases. Switch roles and try a new destination.
takeaway: Use 'Where is ...?' to ask for a place.
Use straight, left, and right to guide movement.
Use next to and across from to describe a location.
Repeat the direction back if you are unsure.
checkQuestion: Which sign shows where you can ask for help or directions?
teacherNote: Use signs learners are likely to see locally. Explain that real signs may use symbols or another language as well as English.

title: English foundations checkpoint
subject: English
description: Combine greetings, introductions, clarification questions, signs, and directions in one practical challenge.
content: This checkpoint brings the four English lessons together. Review any lesson you need, then complete the questions and the real-world scenario.
goal: Use the English foundations skills together in a realistic first-day situation.
realLifeUse: Use this combined skill when arriving at a new school, training centre, workplace, clinic, or community service.
patterns: Hello. My name is ___.
I am from ___, and I live in ___.
Could you say that again, please?
Where is the ___?
Thank you for your help.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.text: Hello. My name is Zaw. I am here for the computer class.

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.text: Welcome. Please register at the information desk.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.text: What does register mean?

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.text: Write your name on the class list.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.text: I understand. Where is the information desk?

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.text: Go straight. It is next to the classroom.

dialogue.speaker: Learner
dialogue.text: Thank you for your help.

steps: Read the conversation once for meaning.
Read it again and identify the greeting, introduction, clarification question, and direction.
Replace the learner's name and class with your own example.
Practice the conversation aloud, then switch roles.
Complete the quick check before doing the final scenario.

exercises.question: Which sentence is an introduction?
exercises.explanation: 'My name is ...' introduces you to another person.

exercises.question: You do not know the word register. What should you ask?
exercises.explanation: Use 'What does ... mean?' for an unfamiliar word.

exercises.question: Which question helps you find a classroom?
exercises.explanation: Use 'Where is ...?' to ask for a location.

exercises.question: What should you say after receiving directions?
exercises.explanation: Thank the person after they help you.

finalTask: Role-play arriving at a new class. Greet the staff member, introduce yourself, explain which class you need, ask the meaning of one unfamiliar word, ask where the classroom is, repeat the direction, and thank them. Complete the scenario without reading every sentence.
takeaway: You can begin a conversation politely.
You can give a short introduction.
You can ask when you do not understand.
You can ask for and follow simple directions.
checkQuestion: Can you complete the arrival scenario using at least five English sentences?
teacherNote: Observe whether learners can communicate meaning rather than requiring perfect grammar or pronunciation. Let them review earlier lessons before retrying.

title: Greet people and ask them to repeat
subject: Japanese
description: Use polite phrases when meeting someone or when spoken Japanese is difficult to understand.
content: Start with phrases that solve an immediate communication problem. Listen to official audio when possible, then practise the exchange offline.
goal: Greet someone, get their attention, and ask them to repeat.
realLifeUse: Use these phrases in a class, workplace, shop, station, clinic reception area, or community office.

vocabulary.term: おはようございます (ohayou gozaimasu)
よく わかりません (yoku wakarimasen)
もういちど おねがいします (mou ichido onegaishimasu)
ありがとうございます (arigatou gozaimasu)

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: おはようございます。 (Good morning.)

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: おはようございます。

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: [A short instruction in Japanese]

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: すみません。よく わかりません。もういちど おねがいします。

steps: Listen to each phrase twice using the official audio when internet is available.
Say each phrase slowly, then at normal speaking speed.
Practise with one person giving an instruction and the other asking for repetition.
Swap roles and repeat without reading every word.
practice: Choose a class, station, or shop situation. Begin with すみません, say that you do not understand, and ask for one more repetition.

exercises.question: What should you say when you need to hear the sentence again?
options: ありがとうございます
もういちど おねがいします
exercises.explanation: もういちど おねがいします means 'One more time, please.'

finalTask: Complete a four-line role-play: greet someone, listen to an instruction, explain that you do not understand, and ask them to repeat.
takeaway: Use すみません before asking for help.
It is useful and polite to say that you do not understand.
Practise with trusted audio, not romanization alone.
checkQuestion: Can you ask for repetition without reading the full phrase?
teacherNote: Prioritize listening and speaking before writing systems. Use Japan Foundation audio for pronunciation and avoid presenting romanization as a complete substitute for learning Japanese script.

references.title: Irodori Starter: Japanese for Life in Japan

title: Introduce yourself
subject: Japanese
description: Share your name, where you came from, and where you live now in a first meeting.
content: A short introduction helps with a new class, workplace, or community. Use only information you feel comfortable sharing.
goal: Give a short first introduction and respond politely.
realLifeUse: Use this when joining a course, meeting a colleague, or speaking to someone for the first time.

vocabulary.meaning: Nice to meet you / first time meeting

vocabulary.term: わたしは ___ です (watashi wa ___ desu)
ミャンマーから きました (Myanmar kara kimashita)
___ に すんでいます (___ ni sunde imasu)
よろしく おねがいします (yoroshiku onegaishimasu)
vocabulary.meaning: A polite closing used in a first introduction

patterns: はじめまして。わたしは [name] です。
[place] から きました。
いま [place] に すんでいます。
よろしく おねがいします。

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.text: はじめまして。わたしは ミナ です。ミャンマーから きました。

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.text: はじめまして。わたしは ケン です。よろしく おねがいします。

steps: Choose a nickname for practice.
Build a three-line introduction using the patterns.
Listen to official Irodori Lesson 3 audio while online.
Say your introduction twice without rushing.
practice: Work in pairs and swap roles. Do not require learners to share a legal name, address, or immigration details.

exercises.question: Which phrase normally begins a first introduction?
options: もういちど おねがいします
exercises.explanation: はじめまして is used when meeting someone for the first time.

finalTask: Give a four-part introduction: first-meeting greeting, nickname, country or city, and polite closing.
takeaway: A short introduction can be enough.
Use から for where you came from.
Keep private details optional.
checkQuestion: Can you introduce yourself in three or four short lines?
teacherNote: The English meaning of よろしく おねがいします is approximate because there is no single exact equivalent. Teach it as a conventional polite closing here.

title: Buy an everyday item
subject: Japanese
description: Ask whether a shop has an item, ask the price, and say what you want.
content: Shopping language becomes useful quickly. Practise with pictures or safe objects before trying the phrases in a real shop.
goal: Ask for one everyday item and ask its price.
realLifeUse: Use this for food, batteries, stationery, toiletries, or another everyday purchase.

vocabulary.term: ___ は ありますか (___ wa arimasu ka)
これは いくらですか (kore wa ikura desu ka)
___ を ください (___ o kudasai)
vocabulary.meaning: Please give me ___ / I will take ___

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: すみません。でんちは ありますか。 (Excuse me. Do you have batteries?)

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.text: はい、あります。 (Yes, we do.)

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: これは いくらですか。 (How much is this?)

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.text: これを ください。 (I will take this, please.)

steps: Choose one object to buy.
Ask whether the shop has it.
Point to an item and ask the price.
Finish with これを ください and ありがとうございます.
practice: Make a tiny pretend shop with three labelled objects. Take turns being the customer and staff member.

exercises.question: Which question asks the price?
options: これは いくらですか
exercises.explanation: いくら means 'how much' in this shopping question.

finalTask: Role-play buying one item: get attention, ask if it is available, ask the price, choose it, and thank the staff member.
takeaway: Begin politely with すみません.
Use いくらですか to ask a price.
Check the displayed price as well as listening.
checkQuestion: Can you ask for an item and its price?
teacherNote: Use real price labels and calculators where helpful. Do not expect mastery of Japanese counters in this starter activity.

title: Check a bus or train
subject: Japanese
description: Ask whether public transport goes to your destination and confirm a location.
content: Transport questions are easier when you combine short Japanese with a written destination, map, or phone screen.
goal: Ask whether a bus or train goes to a destination.
realLifeUse: Use this at a bus stop, station, ticket counter, or information desk.

vocabulary.term: この バスは ___ に いきますか (kono basu wa ___ ni ikimasu ka)
___ は どこですか (___ wa doko desu ka)

dialogue.speaker: Traveller
dialogue.text: すみません。この バスは くうこうに いきますか。 (Does this bus go to the airport?)

dialogue.speaker: Staff
dialogue.text: はい、いきます。 (Yes, it does.)

dialogue.speaker: Traveller
dialogue.text: ありがとうございます。

steps: Write or display the destination clearly.
Begin with すみません.
Ask whether this bus goes to the destination.
Listen for はい or いいえ and confirm using a map or sign.
practice: Use a simple map with three destinations. One learner chooses a route; another asks whether it reaches a chosen place.

exercises.question: What should you show while asking about an unfamiliar destination?
options: The written destination or a map
exercises.explanation: A written destination or map can reduce misunderstanding.

finalTask: Plan a short journey on a practice map. Ask about the correct bus, understand a yes or no answer, and thank the helper.
takeaway: Show the destination as well as saying it.
Confirm using signs, maps, or route numbers.
Ask again when the answer is unclear.
checkQuestion: Can you ask if a bus goes to a named destination?
teacherNote: This is language practice, not local transport advice. Verify real routes separately.

title: Practical Japanese checkpoint
subject: Japanese
description: Combine greetings, introductions, shopping, and transport questions in short role-plays.
content: This checkpoint focuses on useful tasks. Clear communication matters more than perfect speed or accent.
goal: Complete four short everyday communication tasks using speech, gestures, and written information.
realLifeUse: Use this review to identify which phrases are ready for real use and which need more listening practice.
steps: Greet someone and ask them to repeat one sentence.
Give a short first introduction.
Ask for one item and its price.
Ask whether a bus goes to a destination.
Review and repeat any difficult task.
practice: Set up four role-play stations. Give simple feedback: message understood, almost understood, or needs another try.

exercises.question: You do not understand an answer. What is the most useful next step?
exercises.explanation: Use もういちど おねがいします to request another repetition.

exercises.question: Which question belongs in a shop?
options: これは いくらですか
この バスは くうこうに いきますか
exercises.explanation: これは いくらですか asks how much an item costs.

finalTask: Complete two role-plays without reading every line: one first meeting and either one shop purchase or one transport question. Use a clarification phrase at least once.
takeaway: Short, clear phrases can solve real problems.
Written destinations and prices support spoken communication.
Continue with official audio and the writing system after these first tasks.
checkQuestion: Which practical situation can you now complete, and which one needs more practice?

resourceGuide.title: Keep the official Irodori course available offline
resourceGuide.description: LearnBridge provides practice and a path. The Japan Foundation provides the full free course materials and trusted audio.
steps: While online, open the official Irodori Starter page.
Download the lesson PDFs and matching MP3 ZIP files.
Extract the MP3 files and test one recording before going offline.
On phones and tablets, use separate MP3 files because audio embedded in a PDF may not play.

teacherNote: Ask a competent Japanese speaker to review local adaptations before group use. Keep official files outside LearnBridge unless their license permits the planned distribution.

references.title: About Irodori: Japanese for Life in Japan

title: Calm breathing
subject: Wellbeing
description: A short calming activity for stressful learning days.
content: Sit comfortably if you can. Breathe in slowly while counting 1, 2, 3. Breathe out slowly while counting 1, 2, 3. Repeat five times. Notice one thing you can see, one thing you can hear, and one thing you can feel.
goal: Practice a short calming routine for stressful moments.
steps: Sit or stand in a comfortable position if you can.
Breathe in slowly while counting 1, 2, 3.
Breathe out slowly while counting 1, 2, 3.
Repeat five times.
Notice one thing you can see, one thing you can hear, and one thing you can feel.
practice: Do the breathing routine together for one minute. Learners may keep eyes open, look down, sit quietly, or skip the activity if they do not want to join.
checkQuestion: What is one thing you can do when your body feels stressed?
teacherNote: Keep the activity optional and calm. Do not ask learners to explain personal experiences. The goal is a short grounding routine, not counseling.

title: Asking for help
subject: Practical safety
description: Practice how to ask for help from a trusted adult without sharing private details in a group.
content: Children may need help with water, toilets, finding a teacher, feeling unwell, or understanding instructions. This lesson practices simple help-seeking words and safe choices. It does not ask children to describe private family situations.
goal: Ask a trusted adult for help using simple words, pointing, or a help card.
steps: Say together: I need help, please.
Name general trusted helpers in this learning space, such as teacher, volunteer, clinic worker, or community helper.
Practice three safe ways to ask: speaking, pointing, or showing a help card.
Practice choosing a safe place to stand: near the teacher, near the group, or another agreed safe place.
Remember: in a group lesson, you can ask for help without explaining private family details.
practice: Use gentle role-play cards: I need water, I need the toilet, I do not understand, I feel unwell, I cannot find my group. Learners choose a safe helper and practice asking with words, pointing, or a card.
checkQuestion: What is one safe way to ask for help if speaking feels hard?
teacherNote: Keep this protective and non-invasive. Do not ask children to identify personal risks, family problems, legal status, or conflict-related details. Review local referral pathways before using this in a real setting.

references.title: UNICEF: Learning Passport for crisis-affected learning

title: Learning review
subject: Review
description: Review numbers, reading, language, and safety with a short mixed activity.
content: Review what you learned today. Count five objects. Read one sentence. Say one helpful Thai or English word. Name one way to keep personal information private. Mark the lesson complete when you finish.
goal: Review one skill from numbers, reading, language, and safety.
steps: Count five safe objects near you.
Read one short sentence from a lesson.
Say one helpful Thai or English word.
Name one way to keep personal information private.
Choose one lesson you want to practice again.
practice: Learners can answer by speaking, pointing, drawing, writing, or showing objects. The teacher can turn this into a calm group review.
checkQuestion: Which activity felt easiest today, and which one do you want to practice again?
teacherNote: Use this as an end-of-session check. Learners can answer verbally, point, draw, or write depending on age and comfort.

title: Earthquake safety
subject: Emergency safety
description: Practice the widely recommended Drop, Cover, and Hold On action for earthquake shaking.
content: Earthquakes can happen with little warning. During shaking, the main action is Drop, Cover, and Hold On. Drop before shaking knocks you down. Cover your head and neck. Hold on until the shaking stops. After shaking, watch for broken glass, fallen objects, damaged areas, fire, or aftershocks.
goal: Practice Drop, Cover, and Hold On calmly, then review what to check after shaking stops.
steps: Drop down onto hands and knees so shaking does not knock you over.
Cover your head and neck. If a strong table is nearby, get under it. If not, cover with your arms.
Hold on to your shelter or position until the shaking stops.
Do not run outside during shaking. Do not use elevators.
After shaking stops, listen to a trusted adult and move carefully away from broken glass, fallen objects, or damaged areas.
practice: Do a calm 20-second drill. The teacher says, 'Earthquake.' Learners Drop, Cover, and Hold On. Then the teacher says, 'Shaking stopped.' Learners slowly stand, look for hazards, and point to a safe adult or meeting place.
checkQuestion: What are the three words to remember during earthquake shaking?
teacherNote: Practice this as a calm drill, not a frightening story. Adapt the lesson to the building type and local guidance. Ready.gov, ShakeOut, CDC, and UNICEF all recommend Drop, Cover, and Hold On and checking hazards after shaking.

title: When danger is nearby
subject: Emergency safety
description: Practice simple civilian safety steps for loud danger, smoke, or explosions nearby.
content: If you hear danger nearby, stay with your group if it is safe. Move away from windows. Get low and protect your head and neck. Listen for trusted adult instructions. Do not run toward loud sounds, smoke, fire, damaged buildings, or crowds.
goal: Learn calm first actions when loud danger, smoke, or explosions are nearby.
steps: Pause and look for a trusted adult or group leader.
Move away from windows if it is safe to move.
Get low and protect your head and neck.
Stay with your group and listen for trusted adult instructions.
Do not run toward loud sounds, smoke, fire, damaged buildings, or crowds.
practice: Practice with a calm signal. The teacher says, 'Danger nearby.' Learners quietly crouch low, cover head and neck, and point to where a trusted adult would be.
checkQuestion: Should you run toward loud sounds or smoke?
teacherNote: Keep this general and non-tactical. Do not discuss weapons details or local military activity. Review the wording with trusted local protection or education workers before use.

title: Do not touch strange objects
subject: Emergency safety
description: Learn what to do if a child sees unknown metal, wires, shells, or dangerous debris.
content: If you see a strange object, do not touch it. Do not kick it, pick it up, throw it, or take it home. Move away calmly. Tell a trusted adult. Keep other children away if you can do that safely.
goal: Remember the safe rule for unknown objects: do not touch, move away, tell an adult.
steps: Stop before going closer to an unknown object.
Do not touch, kick, pick up, throw, or move the object.
Move away calmly using the same path if it is safe.
Tell a trusted adult what you saw and where you saw it.
Keep other children away only if you can do that safely.
practice: Use a harmless drawing of a strange object. Learners practice saying: Stop. Do not touch. Move away. Tell an adult.
checkQuestion: What should you do first if you see a strange object?
teacherNote: This lesson is for basic unexploded-object awareness. Use simple drawings or safe examples only. Do not show graphic images. Follow local mine-risk or explosive-risk education guidance where available.

title: Emergency bag basics
subject: Emergency safety
description: Learn simple items that families may prepare for emergencies if available.
content: An emergency bag can help if a family needs to move quickly. Useful items may include water, simple food, a flashlight, a whistle, a small cloth, basic medicine managed by an adult, and copies of important papers kept by an adult. Children should ask a trusted adult before packing or using medicine.
goal: Learn what an emergency bag is and why families may prepare one if they can.
steps: Ask a trusted adult where emergency items are kept.
Name simple useful items: water, simple food, flashlight, whistle, cloth, and adult-managed medicine.
Remember that important papers and medicine should be handled by adults.
Keep the bag in a place adults choose and children can remember.
Do not feel ashamed if your family does not have every item.
practice: Look at a picture or list of items. Learners choose three items that could help in an emergency and explain why.
checkQuestion: Who should manage medicine and important papers?
teacherNote: Present this as optional and realistic. Some families may not have these items. Avoid making learners feel ashamed if they cannot prepare a bag.
